metadata.title: Predicting the Mathematics Literacy of Resilient Students from High‐performing Economies: A Machine Learning Approach

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses PISA 2022 microdata and defines an analytic subgroup of resilient students within each economy based on ESCS (bottom quarter) and mathematics literacy (top quarter). The authors explicitly incorporate final student weights (W_FSTUWT) into the ML model development and validation to account for PISA’s complex survey design, including stratification and clustering and unequal selection probabilities. This weighting is intended to make the ML predictions representative of the target student population within each culture group (Eastern vs Western). The manuscript does not report replicate-weight procedures (e.g., BRR/jackknife), but it does state that W_FSTUWT is used during training/validation, so the reported performance should be interpreted as weight-adjusted rather than purely unweighted.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: From PISA 2022, resilient students are selected within each economy using OECD guidance: (1) ESCS-disadvantaged students are those in the bottom quarter of ESCS within their own economy; (2) among these, students are further restricted to those whose mathematics literacy is in the top quarter within their economy. To define the top quarter of mathematics literacy, the authors compute an average of 10 mathematics plausible values (PV1–PV10) per student, rank students by this average, and select the top 25% within each economy. The final analytic sample is then split into culture groups using Triandis’ (1995) Eastern vs Western classification and combined into two datasets (Eastern n=1063; Western n=3591), totaling n=4654 resilient students across the listed high-performing mathematics economies. Missing questionnaire/well-being feature values are imputed using missForest (RF-based imputation) before ML training.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Mathematics literacy (resilient students; Eastern cultures subset)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 mathematics literacy data for resilient students in Eastern cultures, the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy (21st-century and formal/applied), mathematics anxiety, effort/persistence, and working in the household to predict mathematics literacy with Random Forest, finding that predictive accuracy was lower than in Western cultures (e.g., PV1 test RMSE=44.47; PV10 test R2=0.20). This indicates that Eastern-culture resilience in mathematics is more weakly predictable from the selected individual-level questionnaire features, suggesting that interventions may need broader or more context-specific supports beyond self-efficacy and anxiety alone.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Mathematics literacy (resilient students; Eastern cultures subset)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 mathematics literacy data for resilient students in Eastern cultures, the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy (21st-century and formal/applied), mathematics anxiety, effort/persistence, and working in the household to predict mathematics literacy with Lasso Regression, finding that predictive fit remained low (e.g., PV1 test R2=0.00; PV5 test R2=0.06) and was weaker than in Western cultures. This indicates that linear, sparsity-regularized relationships between the selected questionnaire features and resilient mathematics literacy are less stable in Eastern contexts, implying that interventions may require additional predictors (e.g., school/system factors) or non-linear modeling of emotional and instructional mechanisms.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Mathematics literacy (resilient students; Western cultures subset)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 mathematics literacy data for resilient students in Western cultures, the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy (formal), family support, home possessions, mathematics anxiety, and cognitive activation (encouraging mathematical thinking) to predict mathematics literacy with Random Forest, finding that model performance was stronger than in Eastern cultures (e.g., PV1 test RMSE=42.27; PV10 test R2=0.08; MAE around 31.61–33.57). This indicates that Western-culture resilience in mathematics is more closely aligned with self-efficacy and supportive home/learning environments, suggesting that policy and school practice should prioritize self-efficacy-building and family/home engagement strategies for disadvantaged-but-high-achieving students.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2022 Mathematics literacy (resilient students; Western cultures subset)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2022 mathematics literacy data for resilient students in Western cultures, the study leveraged mathematics self-efficacy (formal), family support, home possessions, mathematics anxiety, and cognitive activation (encouraging mathematical thinking) to predict mathematics literacy with Lasso Regression, finding better predictive performance than in Eastern cultures (e.g., PV1 test RMSE=40.25; PV1 test R2=0.11). This indicates that Western-culture resilient mathematics literacy is more consistently associated with self-efficacy and supportive learning/home conditions, suggesting that targeted self-efficacy interventions and supportive family engagement may be effective for disadvantaged high performers.

data.outcome_summary: The study uses PISA 2022 mathematics literacy data to predict mathematics literacy among resilient students (n=4654) selected within each economy as ESCS bottom-quarter but mathematics top-quarter, then grouped into Eastern (n=1063) and Western (n=3591) cultures. The dependent variable is mathematics plausible values (PV1–PV10), with selection based on the average of 10 PVs and model evaluation reported across PVs. Two supervised ML models—Random Forest and Lasso Regression—were trained using missForest (RF-based) single imputation for missing features and nested cross-validation (5×5 outer/inner folds). Performance was evaluated with RMSE, R², and MAE; both models performed better in Western cultures than Eastern cultures (e.g., Random Forest PV1 test RMSE=42.27 vs 44.47; Lasso PV1 test R²=0.11 vs 0.00). The most important predictors differed by culture: Eastern cultures emphasized mathematics self-efficacy (21st-century and formal) and mathematics anxiety, while Western cultures emphasized mathematics self-efficacy (formal) and family/home supports. Because the analysis is predictive (not causal) and uses questionnaire-level individual features only, results should be interpreted as correlational patterns rather than evidence of causal effects.
